quick.summary: How to stop bad records from ruining your business dashboards.
quick.takeaway: Load records into a hidden area and test them before users see them.

parts.title: Taste before serving

beats.line: A broken date field wrecked our dashboard today. How did that slip through?
You served the meal before tasting it.
The pipeline runs automatically every morning. I was asleep.
A good kitchen has a tasting spoon.
You load the new records into a hidden staging area first.
Then you run checks. Are there blanks? Are dates in the future?
And if the soup tastes bad, we throw it out?
You pause the pipeline and alert the team.
But what happens to the dashboard while we fix the broken soup?

parts.cliff: How to keep dashboards alive when pipelines break.

beats.line: The dashboard keeps showing the data from yesterday.
So the bad records never reach the business users.
Exactly right. We call this the write audit publish pattern.
Can I just say taste before serving?
I love it. Taste before serving.
You only move data to production if all the checks pass.
What if a small error is okay? Like one missing zip code.
You can set rules. Warn on small things, stop on big ones.
So I write to staging, check the dates, and publish if clean.
Now you are cooking with quality data.

quiz.question: What is the primary benefit of staging data before making it available to users?
options: It gives you a chance to verify data quality in secret.
It makes the database run queries much faster.
It automatically fixes any missing values it finds.
It compresses the data to save storage costs.
quiz.explanation: Staging hides the loading process. This lets you test the data and block bad records from ruining public reports.

quiz.question: If a pipeline stops because of a data error, the business dashboard must go blank.
quiz.explanation: By checking data before publishing, the dashboard simply continues to show the last known good data until the issue is fixed.
